text:
Sampled ranking can hide difficult competition: strong separation from random items does not establish strong full-catalog ranking. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) show sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons, even in expectation. [RecSys 2025 research](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) further distinguishes sampling resolution, fidelity, robustness and predictive power; candidate composition changes what an evaluation measures. Hard candidate sets therefore provide stress tests, not corrected estimates of full-catalog performance.

For the single HSTU model, a useful diagnostic design is to freeze equal-sized candidate sets containing uniform unseen items, training-frequency-matched items, and title/description-similar items. Report held-out positive rank distributions, score margins and rank degradation across sets, stratified by positive-item training frequency. This is a proposed application of the evidence, not an established benchmark. Semantically similar unseen items remain unobserved candidates, not confirmed negatives; [SIGIR 2026 work](https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/1775773) explicitly identifies false negatives as a problem with hard-negative mining.

Measure embedding hubness through item k-occurrence—appearances in other items’ nearest-neighbor lists—as defined in [scikit-hubness](https://scikit-hubness.readthedocs.io/en/latest/documentation/analysis.html). Separately measure recommendation exposure concentration, catalog coverage, cross-user list overlap and within-list textual similarity, broken down by training-frequency strata. Geometric hubs and frequently recommended items need not coincide. Keep these descriptive diagnostics separate from unchanged host validation HR@10; use only the trained HSTU scores, with no popularity or transition-score fusion.
